Front: How long do you have to complete a patient care record/report (PCR)?
Back: PCR must be completed within 24 hours of disposition of the incident

Front: Under what circumstances may the medical director revoke a credential to practice as noted in the COGs? Be able to explain each of these in some detail.
Back:
1. Lapse, Loss, or Suspension of applicable Certification or Licensure from International Academies of Emergency Dispatch (IAED) or Texas Department of State Health Service (TDSHS)
  2. Separation from All System Registered Responder Organizations
  3. Any action taken against the provider’s certification/license by the certifying/licensing body (administrative review, suspension, etc.)
  4. Arrest for a crime that meets the reporting requirements
  5. FMLA/Military or other voluntary leave
  6. Failure to complete patient care reports in a timely manner (notice at 7 days, administrative hold at 14 days)
Document: OCMO Modification or Revocation of Credential to Practice

Front: Explain when you would utilize the atypical clinical guideline and online medical direction
Back:
Use this guideline for complicated or unusual encounters either:
  1. When a case is covered by a guideline but needs operational or administrative clarification
  2. When no guideline covers the situation and online medical control orders are needed. Contact the designated clinical supervisor first through Communications, and if medical control is needed contact the on-call System Medical Director or receiving hospital physician on a recorded line, then document names, times, and consultation details in the PCR
Document: Atypical Guideline Utilization and Online Medical Direction

Front: Under what circumstances can a provider cancel or alter a response?
Back:
After patient assessment, any on-scene credentialed provider may modify or cancel the response mode of any other system provider not already on scene. Additional specifics include:
  1. Before arrival, EMS specialty units with at least one provider at PL5 or higher (or OCMO providers) may replace an assigned ambulance on priority 4 or 5 calls except PSYC4F, respond non-emergency, and request transport if needed
  2. C4 credentialed providers may cancel units on calls triaged to C4
  3. If cancelled, responders may reduce to non-lights/sirens and still assist as appropriate

Front: Explain specifics related to cardiac arrest documentation
Back: For every cardiac arrest, document and narrate as many key elements as possible including team leader/unit, witnessed status, pre-arrest circumstances, patient description, bystander CPR, unusual findings, patient response, and major interventions. Verbalize and record interventions such as compressions start-stop and compressor switches, AED/monitor decisions, CPR feedback use, ventilation details, EtCO2 values and waveform, advanced airway placement and confirmation, pulse checks during rhythm analysis, medications, and ROSC

Front: Explain what you will do if the patient is obviously deceased when you arrive
Back: If the patient is pulseless and apneic and meets obvious death criteria (such as decomposition, decapitation, severe incineration, obviously mortal wounds, prolonged submersion, trauma with no signs of life, dependent lividity, or rigor mortis), do not initiate or continue resuscitation and document the specific criteria in the ePCR. Follow dead-on-scene crime scene management: if not credentialed to seek TOR, leave via the path of entry without touching anything. If TOR is required, only one properly credentialed provider should enter
Document: Criteria for Death or Withholding Resuscitation

Front: Discuss crime scene management
Back:
Crime scene management depends on the situation:
  1. No resuscitation initiated: non-credentialed responders leave by path of entry without touching anything. Only one properly credentialed provider enters when TOR is needed
  2. Unsuccessful resuscitation: after TOR, immediately vacate area and mark unsuccessful IV/IO or pleural decompression attempts on the body
  3. Patient transport: leave removed clothing, jewelry, or other objects on scene and document/report locations to law enforcement, avoid cutting through existing clothing defects, notify receiving facility if sheet/personal effects may be evidence. If law enforcement is absent, first response agency remains outside perimeter until arrival
  4. Exigent movement: do not disturb or remove body without medical examiner authorization except statutory exceptions. If movement is requested, use evidence blankets when possible and preserve evidence

Front: Can we cover a decedent with a blanket from their home (hint: no)
Back: No. Never use items from the incident scene, including home blankets or sheets. A decedent may be covered only in coordination with law enforcement and only with a trace-evidence blanket when requested by law enforcement

Front: Explain under what circumstances and how we must report abuse and/or neglect of individuals aged 18 or older
Back: For individuals 18 years or older, report when suspicious partner violence or elder abuse findings are present, including psychological indicators, physical injuries inconsistent with mechanism, or signs of neglect. Report immediately to DFPS hotline 800-252-5400. If patient refuses, report as soon as reasonably possible after leaving scene. If transported, report after transfer of care at the hospital. Notify receiving RN or physician of findings and document DFPS intake or case number in the PCR

Front: Explain under what circumstances and how we must report abuse and/or neglect of individuals aged under 18
Back: For individuals younger than 18 years old, report when child abuse or neglect is suspected, especially when injuries or illness are not consistent with reported history. Healthcare providers are obligated to report to local law enforcement or the TDFPS hotline 800-252-5400 and should do so immediately. Complete reporting as soon as reasonably possible after transfer if needed, do not make the report in front of parent or caregiver, and notify receiving RN or physician when transported. Document who received the report and add an addendum if reporting occurs after PCR completion

Front: Explain the process we would follow to report abuse and/or neglect
Back: Stabilize and treat injuries first, then request law enforcement as needed for safety. Do not initiate the report in front of the patient, parent, or caregiver. Report to Texas Department of Family and Protective Services using the hotline 800-252-5400 as soon as reasonably possible, typically after transfer of care if transported. Notify receiving hospital staff of scene concerns and document who was notified and when. Include DFPS intake or case number in the PCR when applicable

Front: Explain how you would document suspected child (or any age) abuse
Back: Document objective findings in detail, including exact quoted statements from the patient, parent, or caregiver, abnormal behaviors, scene and environment conditions, and who received the abuse report. Record reporting date and time and reporting destination. If reporting occurs after PCR completion, add an addendum with those reporting details. Include DFPS intake or case number for encounters reported to DFPS

Front: There are four guiding principles regarding the assessment and treatment of the abused child, be able to list and discuss.
Back:
The four guiding principles are
  1. Protect the child from harm
  2. Suspect abuse especially when injury or illness is not consistent with reported history
  3. Respect the privacy of the child and family
  4. Collect and document as much information as possible

Front: What is child abuse?
Back: Under CAPTA, child abuse and neglect means any recent act or failure to act by a parent or caretaker that results in death, serious physical or emotional harm, sexual abuse, or exploitation, or an act or failure to act that presents an imminent risk of serious harm

Front: Explain general crime scene principles
Back: General principles include initiating indicated resuscitation even on a possible crime scene, limiting scene contact to what patient care requires, avoiding use of any scene items, minimizing handling of evidence and documenting any moved items, discouraging victims from washing or cleaning up, handling weapons only when necessary with gloves and documentation, and following TOR and medical examiner jurisdiction requirements once resuscitation stops

Front: Under what circumstances would we withhold resuscitation?
Back: Withhold resuscitation only when the patient is obviously dead by criteria or has a valid out of hospital DNR. If unsure, resuscitate. In a pulseless apneic patient this includes findings such as decomposition, decapitation, severe incineration, obviously mortal wounds, prolonged submersion greater than 20 minutes, blunt or penetrating trauma with no signs of life, dependent lividity, or rigor mortis in major joints
Document: Criteria for Death or Withholding Resuscitation

Front: Under what circumstances can a BLS provider contact communications for a Time of Death (TOD)?
Back: A BLS provider may contact communications for time of death when resuscitative care was not initiated or continued and death criteria are met, after confirming pupils are fixed and dilated, carotid or femoral pulse is absent for 30 seconds, and apical heart sounds are absent for 30 seconds
Document: Criteria for Death or Withholding Resuscitation

Front: What is the definition of a patient?
Back: A patient is any individual, or a person called about by a third party, who has a complaint suggestive of potential illness or injury, requests evaluation for potential illness or injury, has obvious evidence of illness or injury, has had an acute event that could reasonably lead to illness or injury, or is in a circumstance that could reasonably lead to illness or injury

Front: Explain what “Against Medical Advice” (AMA) means
Back: AMA means a patient with present mental capacity chooses to refuse recommended evaluation, treatment, and or transport after being informed of relevant risks, benefits, and alternatives. Adults with present mental capacity retain the right to refuse care and or transport against medical advice
Document: Refusal of Treatment and or Transport

Front: Describe “present mental capacity” and steps for assessing capacity
Back:
Present mental capacity is the ability of an eligible patient to make an informed decision to accept or refuse care. The patient must be 18 years or older or an emancipated minor, not suicidal or homicidal, and not stripped of decision-making by a court. For refusal to be accepted, the patient must demonstrate all four:
  1. Understands their illness or injury and the benefits of treatment and or evaluation
  2. Understands the consequences, including death, of not seeking treatment and or evaluation
  3. Understands the alternatives to immediate care by EMS
  4. Can describe these components in their own words and provide a defined reason for refusing treatment and or transport
Use the Determination of Capacity checklist, contact Online Medical Control if there is uncertainty or if capacity is lacking, and document history and exam allowed, absence of suicidal or homicidal ideation, assessment components, and any Online Medical Control contact

Front: Who is a minor in the State of Texas, and why is this important?
Back: A minor is a person under 18 years old who is not and has never been married, or who has not had disabilities of minority removed by a court for general purposes. This matters because minors generally cannot consent to or refuse treatment, may need an appropriate consenter, and may require refusal documentation rather than designation as no patient when no consenter is available

Front: Under what circumstances can a minor accept or refuse treatment/transport?
Back: A minor can consent to or refuse when legally emancipated. A minor may also consent in specific situations without a parent or guardian, including active duty military status, age 16 or older and living separately while managing own financial affairs, diagnosis and treatment of reportable infectious disease, pregnancy related care excluding abortion, treatment related to drug or alcohol dependency, and care for their biological child if unmarried and has custody

Front: What is “emancipation”?
Back: Emancipation is a court granted removal of the disabilities of minority that gives a minor adult rights for medical consent and refusal. In this standard, a minor is considered emancipated if they have obtained a Texas court order of emancipation

Front: Describe the criteria for a pediatric patient
Back: For transport destination decisions, pediatric is any patient younger than 18 years old unless another guideline states otherwise. For selecting treatment guidelines, pediatric is any patient under 37 kg or a patient who can be measured using a PEDIA Tape

Front: Under what circumstances can a provider discontinue prehospital resuscitation?
Back: Unsuccessful CPR and advanced life support interventions may be discontinued prior to transport after adequate and appropriate greater than PL4 therapy and checklist use. For ongoing resuscitation over 30 minutes, inclusion criteria include adequate CPR, managed airway with placement verification, IV or IO access, rhythm appropriate medications and defibrillation, ultrasound when available, and provider agreement, then a greater than PL5 provider contacts OLMC for TOR. A greater than PL5 provider may also seek TOR before 30 minutes based on presentation and clinical judgment. Continue resuscitation and transport in special higher-survival situations such as suspected hypothermia, sustained ROSC, persistent VF or pulseless VT or ongoing neurologic activity, or cardiac motion on ultrasound

Front: Explain the guideline related to Out of Hospital DNRs (OOHDNR)
Back: If presented with a completed OOH-DNR form or OOH-DNR identification device, providers should withhold CPR and listed therapies during cardiac arrest and honor terminal wishes. If uncertain about criteria, resuscitate and contact OLMC. Begin resuscitation until directed otherwise when the patient is pregnant, circumstances are suspicious or unnatural, DNR validity is uncertain, or clarification is needed. OOH-DNR may be original or copy and may come from any US state. A DNR may be revoked by the patient or person who executed the order by destroying the form or device, stating intent to revoke, or physician documented revocation

Front: Under what circumstances do we NOT honor an OOHDNR?
Back: Do not honor an OOHDNR when exceptions apply. Begin resuscitation until directed otherwise if the patient is known to be pregnant, there are indications of unnatural or suspicious circumstances, the existence or validity of the DNR is uncertain, or there is question about whether to honor the order. If unsure, resuscitate and contact OLMC

Front: Under what circumstances can a DNR be overridden?
Back: A DNR can be overridden when the patient or person who executed the order revokes it by destroying the form or directing removal of the identification device, or by telling EMS or the attending physician they intend to revoke it. It can also be overridden when the attending physician or designee documents revocation in the medical record with time, date, and place and marks each page VOID

Front: Under what circumstances must you complete a PCR?
Back: Complete an ePCR for dispatched incidents involving patient contact or when required dispositions apply, with the goal of one ePCR per incident whenever a CAD medical request is generated, even if care is not delivered. Complete a separate report for each patient when patient contact occurs. If dispatched and replaced by another unit from the same agency before arrival, no ePCR is required

Front: How do you document if you are cancelled prior to arrival?
Back: Select the canceled prior to arrival disposition and document any special circumstances in the narrative. If multiple system organizations responded, at least one credentialed provider from each organization must complete a report accurate to that organization activities

Front: How do you document if you do not make patient contact?
Back: Select the no patient contact disposition. If the patient could not be located, document efforts made to locate the patient in the narrative. If multiple system organizations responded, at least one credentialed provider from each organization must complete a report accurate to that organization activities

Front: What should be included in a PCR?
Back: A PCR should include chief complaint and event history, detailed assessment and rationale, complete physical assessment, initial complete vital signs and pertinent findings, condition-specific details, ongoing monitoring and condition changes, chronological assessments and interventions with results, medication details and response, procedure details such as IV specifics and failed attempts, required monitor strips, requested orders and physician names, narcotic waste documentation when applicable, explanation for any indicated COG action not done, and documentation of all involved credentialed providers and organization specific care

Front: How would you document if an indicated and appropriate assessment, intervention, or action prescribed by the COGs did NOT occur?
Back: Include a clear explanation in the ePCR of why the indicated and appropriate assessment, intervention, or action prescribed by the Clinical Operating Guidelines did not occur

Front: What is included in a complete set of vital signs?
Back: A complete initial set includes pulse rate peripheral or central, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, respiratory rate, pain severity score with scale used plus treatment and response, cumulative GCS with individual subscores, and body temperature

Front: Under what circumstances would you also include pulse oximetry, end-tidal CO2, and ECG monitoring?
Back: Include pulse oximetry, end-tidal CO2, and electrical heart rate from cardiac monitoring based on the patient condition and complaint as clinically indicated

Front: Why should the first blood pressure be manual?
Back: Initial vital signs should be obtained manually to establish a reliable baseline before using electronic measurements. Subsequent electronic values should correlate with the manual set, and if there is discrepancy manual vitals should be continued

Front: Are you required to wear your credential badges on scene?  Why/why not?
Back: Yes. Credential badges should be visibly worn when providing patient care because proper identification is required and helps patients and responders identify credential level and capabilities. Exceptions exist when protective outerwear is required, such as bunker gear or rain gear. Badge display does not replace verbally identifying your role and credentials to the patient and team

Front: Explain what happens if a provider provides care that they are not credentialed to perform.
Back: Practicing outside credentialed scope is a reportable patient safety event and must be reported immediately to the on-duty Designated Medical Officer, Fire Medical Officer, or agency patient safety representative. The event is then handled through the system clinical quality improvement and review process

Front: Discuss the process of medical cross-check and why it’s a patient safety process.
Back: For medication administration, providers use drug formulary dosing references and perform a documented visual verification plus a Medication Administration Cross Check. The checklist is completed independently by a second credentialed provider to verify critical information before administration. This process reduces medication errors and prevents harm by catching mistakes before they reach the patient
Document: Patient Safety and Medication Administration Safety

Front: What must be documented regarding medication administration and medication safety procedures?
Back: Document all medication details completely in the PCR including medication name, dose, route, time, indication, and patient response. Also document completion of medication safety procedures, including visual verification and medication administration cross-check per the medication safety standard

Front: What equipment/medications must be IMMEDIATELY available at the patient’s bedside at your PL level?
Back: Minimum to patient side for all PL levels includes appropriate PPE, defibrillator, stethoscope, BVM with masks, suction, blood pressure cuffs, oxygen with delivery devices, OPA and NPA, intranasal naloxone, oral glucose, tape, 4x4 dressings, Kerlix, mucosal atomization device, and current Clinical Operating Guidelines. Additional requirements are by level: PL2 CPAP, appropriate iGel airway, epinephrine 1 mg/mL with IM supplies, albuterol with nebulizer kit. PL3 saline lock equipment, 250 mL D10W for infusion, naloxone IM or IV. PL4 laryngoscope and blades for FBAO and Magill forceps. PL5 thoracostomy needles, Kelly forceps, and scalpels

Front: Discuss the application of the on-scene authority for patient care clinical standard
Back: When patient care conflicts occur, on-scene credentialed providers should first attempt consensus focused on patient best interest and professionalism. If unresolved, final authority rests with the senior credentialed provider on scene according to the hierarchy, with supervised providers deferring to the assigned training officer at that officer credential level. Significant unresolved conflicts should be reported through clinical event review and to OCMO if care may have been negatively impacted

Front: Discuss the circumstantial evaluation for a patient you are considering referring to an ATU, MCOT, or psychiatric ED
Back: Circumstantial evaluation requires all of the following before referral: the patient understands and follows commands, does not require physical restraints, is not in custody of a peace officer, and no physician has specifically requested ambulance transport. Referral also requires meeting general applicability and vital sign requirements and having no immediate exclusion criteria
Document: Patient Referral to ATU MCOT Psychiatric ED

Front: Discuss, in some detail, the patient safety standard.
Back: The patient safety standard directs safe equipment and clinical practices to reduce errors and patient harm. It requires medication dose verification and cross-check, visible credentials, beginning-of-shift verification of required equipment and supplies, restocking when depleted, and remaining out of service when major depletion or contamination occurs. Equipment failures during patient care must be removed from service and reported. Near misses, clinical errors, and adverse events must be reported as soon as possible through the defined notification sequence to support continuous improvement and safer care

Front: What MUST be reported as a patient safety event?
Back: Mandatory reporting includes immediate reports for medication or procedural errors with known or suspected harm, harmful equipment failures or missing equipment, patient injury while in system care, in-custody death, unrecognized esophageal intubation, provider impairment on duty, potentially avoidable patient injury in EMS care, practice outside credentialed scope, altered or disregarded medical control orders, and suspected EMTALA violations. Report within 12 hours events such as errors with potential harm, equipment failures changing care, inability to complete therapy due to equipment issues, regulatory reportable events, franchise provider calls to 911 for a patient in their care, any cardiac arrest in presence of system providers, and concerns about care by other healthcare providers

Front: A physician arrives on the scene. What must he/she present to participate in patient care?
Back: A non-system EMS physician on scene should appropriately identify themselves with a Texas Medical Board wallet card or other identifying device. Care must be appropriate to the circumstances, documented by EMS including physician name, and when possible coordinated with OLMC

Front: A physician on scene is asking you to do something that is outside your scope. What do you do?
Back: Work within the Clinical Operating Guidelines and your credentialed scope, assist the physician only within those limits, and contact OLMC immediately if issues arise. Care by an on-scene non-system physician should be coordinated with OLMC whenever possible

Front: What is an “intervener physician,” and what options does this person have if they wish to participate in patient care?
Back: An intervener physician is an on-scene physician who is not a system EMS physician and seeks to direct or participate in care. To participate, they should identify themselves with TMB wallet card or similar identification, provide care appropriate to circumstances, have their involvement documented by EMS, and coordinate with OLMC when possible. System providers continue working within COGs while assisting for patient benefit

Front: Explain implied consent.
Back: Implied consent applies in potentially life-threatening emergencies when the patient cannot provide informed consent and the law presumes they would consent if able. This includes inability to communicate due to injury, illness, accident, or altered mental status, impaired present mental capacity, or a minor with life-threatening illness or injury when no parent, conservator, or guardian is present
Document: Refusal of Treatment and or Transport

Front: Explain informed consent/refusal
Back: Informed consent and refusal require that the patient has adequate reasoning capacity and receives relevant information about risks, benefits, and consequences. The patient must understand facts, implications, and future consequences of the decision and available options if they decline evaluation or treatment
Document: Refusal of Treatment and or Transport

Front: What is substituted (surrogate) consent?
Back: Substituted or surrogate consent is consent given by an individual with legal standing when the patient cannot consent, such as when the patient is a minor, incarcerated, or legally incompetent. Parents or guardians may consent for a child and are presumed to act in the child best interest absent abuse or neglect
Document: Refusal of Treatment and or Transport

Front: Explain, in some detail, application of the refusal of treatment and/or transport standard.
Back: Refusal application requires confirming legal eligibility and capacity. Patients refusing must be adults or emancipated minors, have present mental capacity, not be court-declared incompetent, and not be suicidal or homicidal. Patients meeting criteria may refuse any or all treatment or transport. Providers should encourage care, may involve additional resources including physician, supervisor, paramedic practitioner, or OLMC, and must not deny requested treatment or transport without OLMC and PINT process compliance
Document: Refusal of Treatment and or Transport

Front: What things must you consider if a patient with capacity wishes to refuse care?
Back: Confirm the patient has present mental capacity, legal authority to refuse, and no disqualifiers such as court declared incompetence or suicidal or homicidal status. Ensure refusal is informed by discussing risks, benefits, incomplete prehospital evaluation limits, and alternatives. Encourage care and consider involving physician, command staff, or OLMC for support and risk reduction
Document: Refusal of Treatment and or Transport

Front: What documentation needs to be included for a patient who wants to refuse care?
Back: Document the refusal encounter in the PCR including capacity assessment elements, informed refusal discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives, and pertinent history and exam permitted by the patient. Document absence of suicidal or homicidal ideation when assessed, reason for refusal in patient own words when possible, and any consultation with OLMC or supervisors
Document: Refusal of Treatment and or Transport

Front: Describe how you would perform CPSS and VAN assessments.
Back: Perform CPSS completely by checking all CPSS components and treat any abnormal CPSS finding as stroke positive. If CPSS is positive then assess for weakness and perform VAN. Any positive VAN component is VAN positive. Positive CPSS plus weakness plus positive VAN indicates LVO

Front: Why must you get a blood glucose before calling a stroke alert?
Back: Blood glucose must be obtained before declaring a stroke alert because stroke and LVO alert pathways require glucose assessment and alert criteria include blood glucose greater than 50, helping identify mimics and support correct destination decisions

Front: Briefly discuss the System Performance Improvement standard and your part in it.
Back: The standard requires all system agencies and providers to actively participate in continuous performance improvement through performance measures, preplanning and post-implementation evaluation, review of clinical errors and concerns, and participation in external registries and systems of care programs. Your role is to self-report, provide constructive feedback, and participate in improvement processes consistently, since failure to participate can result in credential consequences

Front: Can someone with a PL4 or higher transfer patient care to you?  If yes, under what circumstances?
Back: Yes. A higher credentialed provider may transfer care to a lesser credentialed provider when immediate transport of a critical patient is needed and the established care left with you is within your scope, training, and equipment capability. This should not be routine and requires that all patients are accounted for, assessed, and triaged with additional resources requested. Patients requiring immediate advanced stabilization must not be left unless an appropriately credentialed and equipped provider can perform that care
Document: Transfer of Care to Provider of Lesser Credentials
